newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebel head has serious skin disease - sources.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebel head has serious skin disease - sources.

text.p: Peru's Maoist Shining Path rebel leader is seriously ill, suffering from a rare skin disease that has left his body riddled with parasites as he hides out in the isolated Andes, anti-terrorist police sources said on Saturday.

Oscar Ramirez, alias "Feliciano," has a tropical disorder caused by mosquito bites that leave a corrosive saliva burrowing deep holes throughout the skin, members of a special anti-terrorist police team hunting for the guerrilla said.
The contagious disease, known as uta, which is caught in jungle highland regions, can be cured, but without treatment the debilitating illness can eventually kill, doctors said.

"The guy is really ill. His condition is very advanced," said one source, adding that police first received reports Ramirez had uta in 1991. The illness -- particularly serious in the rebel's throat -- has worsened in recent months, he said.
Hiding in a remote zone in one of the most backward areas of Peru, police doubt the guerrilla leader receives treatment for the disease, the sources said.

Police hope Ramirez's condition will force him to seek treatment, as did Hector Bejar, a former rebel leader in the now-defunct National Liberation Army group, who was captured in 1965 when he left his jungle hide-out to seek medical aid for uta.

Ramirez is believed to live nomadically in extremely cold mountains on the edge of the central jungle forest around an area so isolated it is not named on maps. Known locally as "Vizcatan," the zone, 360 miles (570 km) east of Lima, lies two days walk from the nearest track accessible to motor vehicles at the source of the river Apurimac in the central department of Ayacucho, the sources said.
Gen. Nicolas Hermoza, Peru's military chief, called Vizcatan Shining Path's "last refuge" as he reviewed the army's manoeuvres in the the zone while on a visit on Friday.

For more than a week, Peru's army has been carrying out a massive hunt for Ramirez and other Shining Path leaders as well as the group's secret arms caches in Ayacucho and the Huallaga valley, 450 miles (720 km) to the north.

Deploying over 100 soldiers and 40 anti-terrorist police officers, the army last week captured four key military leaders controlling two 200-strong units and a huge arsenal of rocket launchers, grenades and rifles deep in the Huallaga jungle.
So far the Ayacucho arm of the operation has yielded few results apart from the capture of at least one high-ranking rebel, military sources said.
Last September, the army carried out a similar hunt for Ramirez, but he slipped through a ring of 2,000 soldiers in the central Andes.

"Comrade Feliciano" has gradually come to dominate the Shining Path -- greatly weakened since the 1992 capture of its leader Abimael Guzman -- and has steered the group to a bloodier course over the last two years, security forces say.

The man-hunt for the commander-in-the-field coincides with the group's recent attacks in Lima that raised fears Shining Path was beginning a new campaign of violence. Last week, guerrillas exploded a huge car bomb at a police station in a shanty town, injuring at least eight officers, and on Tuesday shot to death one policeman patrolling a suburb.
